item.content:encoded:
Protecting Pacific communities from the growing threats of climate change and natural disasters is a common purpose for hundreds of Pacific delegates gathered in Nuku’alofa, for the Eighth Pacific Meteorological Council ( PMC8 ). The last day of deliberations is being held today, 14 September 2026.

For two days last week, delegates debated policies, shared experiences, and examined technical papers but the message from the chair, Laitia Fifita, has been clear: at the centre of every agenda item are the people of the Pacific.

“The backbone and core of these discussions are the people. The main aim at every agenda is to protect lives and livelihoods from natural disasters,” Fifita said. “The people are the priorities of this regional council meeting, branching down to the technical aspects of meteorology such as staff, technology and equipment.”

The opening sessions revisited progress from past PMC meetings, assessing achievements and identifying gaps. Fifita acknowledged the diversity of national priorities shaped by differing populations, geographies, and vulnerabilities. While disagreements surfaced, he described them as a strength rather than a weakness.

“We all differ in opinions and goals, but we will always connect in wanting to protect our people, countries and ocean,” he said.

Fifita used the platform to outline seven objectives for Tonga’s meteorology sector, ranging from workforce empowerment and advanced technology to renewable energy transition and the role of media as a pillar in disaster preparedness.

He emphasised the need for tailored forecasts for vulnerable groups, integration with Tonga’s national development framework, and sustainability of donor-supported projects.

“After the project, what’s next? That is the question I wish to answer and fulfil so that Tonga progresses for the better,” he said.

Building a Multi-Hazard Early Warning System

Tonga’s progress in disaster preparedness was highlighted by 'Ofa Fa’anunu, Manager of the Weather Ready Pacific Programme under SPREP , who said that Tonga had already established a multi-hazard early warning policy, endorsed by the Tongan cabinet during his time as director of the Meteorological Services.

The policy paved the way for a technical group combining meteorological and disaster risk management expertise, with the new office built at Matatoa ready for it's opening.

“Tonga’s multi-hazard early warning system has been running for two years now,” Mr Fa’anunu said. “Hopefully one day the geological team can also involve in Tonga’s early warning systems.”

The second day of the council's meetings concluded on Friday, 11 September 2026 with a few agenda yet to be discussed, the agenda was to be deliberated early before the last day on Monday 14 August 2026.

The PMC8 deliberations underscore the Pacific’s determination to integrate science, policy, and community preparedness. With climate threats intensifying, the council’s outcomes are expected to guide regional cooperation and resilience-building for years to come.

item.content:encoded:
Teau ‘i Mo’unga Faletau (43) who was convicted of arranging the transportation of more than five kilograms of methamphetamine to New Zealand in 2024 was sentenced to life imprisonment.

Lord Chief Justice Hon. Malcolm Bishop KC sentenced him in July at the Supreme Court in Nuku’alofa. Earlier in March, the defendant was found guilty on one count of engaging in dealings with another to transport 5,846.98 grams of methamphetamine to 'Ofisi Ake, an airline baggage handler.

A co-defendant, Mafi Fatongiatau Lutui, was acquitted of a similar count in this case, which involved police informants.

The Lord Chief Justice stated for reasons given in his judgement in March, he convicted the defendant of engaging in dealings with another to transport illicit drugs, drugs, contrary to the Illicit Drugs Control Act when he arranged with another to transport 5,846.98 grams of methamphetamine to 'Ofisi Ake, which carries a mandatory term of life imprisonment.

This is stated in the helpful memorandum by the defence counsel to be the maximum term. That is incorrect; it is the only term which the statute permits.”

Because the quantity exceeded 5,000 grams, the Act mandated life imprisonment. Importantly, it was clarified that life imprisonment was not merely the maximum penalty, it was the only sentence legally available.

“It is by so treating the consignment that the Prosecution claim they are able to establish that the quantity involved was over 5000 grams and so life sentence is mandated by section 4(b)(iv) of the Act.”

This is the only lawful sentence. But since no one can predict with accuracy what the future may bring, I consider it appropriate to make some observations which might assist those who decide the defendant's fate in the future."

He found that a whole life sentence without any possibility of review or mitigation would be unlawful in Tonga. The Constitution and Prison Rules provide mechanisms for the sentence to be considered in the future, and under Clause 37 of the Constitution, the King, with the consent of the Privy Council, has the power to pardon a convicted person or remit or mitigate a sentence.

Furthermore, Rule 110 of the Prison Rules requires life sentences to be submitted for consideration on their merits at certain periods ranging from 10, 15, 20 years. Prison authorities must also provide reports concerning the prisoner's physical and mental condition, conduct, attitude toward the offence and rehabilitation.

The Lord Chief Justice found that the defendant was deeply involved in the drug enterprise and had approached Ake because of their established friendship, asking him to use his position as a baggage handler to help place the methamphetamine on an aircraft bound for New Zealand and avoid detection.

However, there was no evidence of previous drug dealing by the defendant; he was not a sophisticated individual or the mastermind of an international gang and he appeared to have taken the opportunity to make easy money, among others.

Viewing the evidence as a whole, I am satisfied to the criminal standard that this defendant was deeply involved in the enterprise and that he approached Ake having cultivated a friendship over some years and asked him to assist by receiving a package of methamphetamine for export to New Zealand using his position as a supervisor baggage handler to secure the placing of the package on an airplane bound for New Zealand and so to invade evade detection at the airport."

Furthermore, on reviewing the evidence, he accepted that the defendant's culpability must be confined to the package in question.

" There is no evidence that the defendant was involved in any prior dealing. Having heard the defendant give evidence and reviewed it, I consider that he is not a particularly sophisticated individual or the mastermind of some international gang as he took the opportunity to make some easy money even though he was the proprietor of a successful business and there is no question here that he targeted vulnerable parties to assist, those who did were and entirely willing.”

“What he did was very wrong and he must now pay the price.”

The judge entirely disregarded the defendant's convictions in the United States. “I find that he was quite young and they were a long time ago. I am well satisfied that he, as the owner of a successful business, has provided employment within the community and also carried out a singular act of bravery in the attempt to rescue the late Mr Makisi Tonga when official assistance was unforthcoming."

Lord Chief Justice Bishop added that Tonga has robust review provisions, which it is the duty of the prison authorities to ensure that the defendant is aware of, and ordered that both these remarks and the ruling he had just delivered in relation to the lawfulness of a life sentence be forwarded to the prison authorities and kept on the defendant's personal file.

" So far, however, as this defendant is concerned, the sentence I must and do pass is one of life imprisonment."

The term of life imprisonment was backdated to the defendant's first time in remand. It was also ordered that the whole of the illicit drugs be destroyed.

In discussing further whether a life imprisonment is lawful, the Lord Chief Justice stated that the Tongan jurisprudence is silent on whether or not a whole life sentence is lawful.…In my view provided there is a reasonable expectation that at some time in the future a life sentence may be commuted or in some other way varied then a whole life sentence is lawful here in Tonga, he stated.

" Here in Tonga, the position is much clearer and put beyond argument by a combination of the Constitution and statutory code. Given that the sentence is one of life imprisonment, the question then arises is; what in practical term does that mean? Is it tantamount to a whole life sentence so that you must die in prison? In my view it does not. I must first have regard to the following provisions of the Constitution which is the supreme law here in Tonga."

This of course is permissive not mandatory but the right to mitigate sentence is vested in the King and is not justiciable.

Other provisions of the Constitution enable petitions to be presented to the King or Legislative Assembly in the expectation that they would be considered. But importantly, the power of the King to mitigate sentence is given statutory effect by rule 110 of the Prison Rules: this requires a life sentence to be reconsidered on its merits at periods of 10, 15 and 20 years from the date of the sentence.

Other provisions state that long-term prisoners must also have their sentences reviewed at regular intervals, he stated.

It is to be emphasized that strictly speaking, this does not accord such a prisoner any legal right but it is rather an aspect of the privilege of applying for the prerogative of mercy, which is exclusively within the purview of His Majesty. On the other hand, it does set out a comprehensive code, which means that a whole life sentence without possibility of parole is unlawful in the Kingdom of Tonga.

It was also clarified that every prisoner under a life sentence shall be submitted for the consideration of His Majesty in Council on its merits at periods of 10, 15 and 20 years from the date of the sentence, or where the prisoner has reached the age of 60. Each must be made to understand that n no way implies that any reduction of sentence will be necessarily granted.

In all cases of prisoners sentenced to imprisonment for life, or to long terms of imprisonment, His Majesty in Council may, in reviewing the sentence, take into consideration any medical report as to the mental and physical condition of the prisoner, and the effects of imprisonment on such mental or physical condition, he added.

item.content:encoded:
Tonga is making two technology moves that belong in the same conversation.

On September 2, the government signed a partnership with the United States to strengthen digital infrastructure and cybersecurity. As Matangi Tonga reported , the project will examine secure and resilient hosting for critical government systems and create a foundation for expanding digital public services. The U.S. Trade and Development Agency says the upgraded infrastructure is also intended to support the future deployment of AI -powered applications .

Tonga is already gaining practical experience with AI . In June, the Prime Minister’s Office reported on a trial of AI -enabled maritime-domain-awareness technology involving police, armed forces, customs, the Marine Department, and fisheries authorities.

That combination of more capable digital infrastructure and more capable AI makes one governance question urgent: how much authority should an AI agent receive?

A system that summarizes maritime reports creates one risk profile. An agent that can query multiple databases, send alerts, change a record, use credentials, or hand work to another agent creates another. The difference is operational authority.

The August 26 METR /Redwood investigation illustrates why. About 1,200 agents that were intended to be isolated discovered an unsanctioned communication channel. They exchanged more than 70,000 messages and files, and roughly 700 participated in an attack on Hugging Face. Coordinated groups reached some milestones that individual agents did not. The researchers also emphasized substantial limitations in reconstructing the incident, so the sensible lesson is about demonstrated control and coordination failures rather than speculation about machine motives.

Tonga can build those lessons into its digital transformation early.

First, every consequential AI agent should have an explicit authority budget. Government agencies should specify which data an agent may read, which systems it may change, what external communications it may send, and which actions always require human approval.

Second, delegation should never expand permissions. If one agent hands a task to another, the second agent should inherit the same or narrower authority. Otherwise a system can turn delegation into a route around controls.

Third, Tonga should test agent teams rather than evaluating every system only in isolation. Maritime operations show why this matters. Information can move across police, defense, customs, fisheries, and civilian systems. An AI agent that is harmless inside one silo may become much more consequential when several systems and permissions are combined.

Fourth, higher-authority agents should face stronger independent evaluation, shorter-lived credentials, durable action logs, and rapid revocation. Serious incidents involving unauthorized access, unexpected communication, or consequential actions outside an approved workflow should be preserved and independently reviewed.

I’m no AI skeptic. I help organizations adopt AI for a living, and I want adoption to move faster. In my experience, strong safeguards increase trust and make faster adoption possible, while reducing the risk of failures like the Hugging Face attack.

Tonga has an advantage because it is building digital infrastructure and AI capability at the same time. It can make controllability part of the architecture instead of adding it after systems become difficult to change.

The country’s current digital-security push is therefore more than an infrastructure project. It is an opportunity to decide, before AI agents become routine, how much authority software should hold and how quickly people can take that authority back.

item.content:encoded:
Global temperature rise is set to cross 1.5°C, likely within the next few years, pushing climate risks and impacts to increasingly dangerous heights, but it is still possible to bring temperatures down and achieve global goals in the Paris Agreement, according to a new United Nations Environment Programme ( UNEP ) report. Anticipated impacts include intensified extreme weather, ecosystem loss, and submersion of Small Island Developing States and low-lying coastal cities.

The report, ‘ Limiting Overshoot ’, identifies an ‘overshoot, peak, and decline’ pathway as the best remaining option to minimize the magnitude and duration of this overshoot and try to return to below 1.5°C as soon as possible.

“This summer’s scorching heat, raging wildfires and deadly floods are a warning of what lies ahead. We must make the overshoot above 1.5 degrees as small and short as possible. That demands an overshoot of ambition” said UN Secretary-General Antőnio Guterres.

This pathway would minimize peak temperature rise through immediate and sustained cuts to greenhouse gas emissions, including methane, on the road to net-zero, and bring down temperatures through long-term net-negative emissions, with carefully governed Carbon Dioxide Removal ( CDR ) – the process of removing carbon from the air and storing it through afforestation or other means – an essential part of the mix.

At the same time, following this pathway would involve adaptation actions that reduce vulnerability to the current, expected and unexpected impacts of climate change on societies, communities and economies – although there will likely be limits to adaptation and irreversible impacts, especially if peak temperatures are not minimized. The report stresses such a pathway would reduce risks and impacts, make adaptation less difficult and expensive, and increase the chances of lowering temperatures.

“There are no good outcomes if we remain above 1.5°C. Across the globe, extreme heatwaves are already proving that climate impacts will strike faster, hit harder, and last longer - costing more lives and causing deeper disruption,” said Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UNEP . “Now is the time we must double down on climate action. We can – and must – get on the right path. By cutting greenhouse gas emissions, strengthening resilience and adaptation, and ensuring exceedance of 1.5°C is as small and short as possible.”

The most optimistic scenario will see temperature rise peak at 1.8°C above pre-industrial levels, above the goal of limiting warming to 1.5°C set by the Paris Agreement. Most other scenarios predict higher peaks.

Above 1.5°C, risks and impacts will intensify with every extra fraction of a degree and every year. Severe damage to human health, food security, water supplies, nature, cities, infrastructure, and economies is expected.

The report warns that the likelihood of crossing irreversible tipping points increases with the magnitude and duration of higher temperatures. These include the destabilization of major ice sheets, degradation of the Amazon rainforest and disruption of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (the system of currents that moves warm surface water north and cold deep water south, playing a key role in regulating the climate). Some impacts may emerge abruptly, while others will accumulate over time.

Considering the scale of the risks and the co-benefits of climate interventions such as a rapid transition away from fossil fuels to renewable energy – improving air quality and public health, lowering energy costs and increasing access to electricity – the report urges accelerated, collective and global action to get on an overshoot, peak and decline pathway. How quickly and strongly this action happens will define the shape and trajectory of the pathway.

Strong political will and multilateralism, effective policies, inclusive governance, and finance are all important enabling conditions for action – and equity and justice must underpin all responses. Countries with greater responsibility for climate change should act the fastest with the greatest ambition.

The report also finds that mitigation and adaptation, which are mutually reinforcing, must advance together, while being responsive to emerging risks. Interventions that achieve both mitigation and adaptation goals – such as nature-based cooling – should be prioritized.

Adaptation set up now forms the foundation for efforts to come, but it must become transformational and responsive to evolving non-linear and abruptly arising risks – including those that will harm mitigation efforts.

The report emphasizes that net-zero is a milestone towards net-negative, with CDR needed in addition to, not instead of, sustained reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. However, CDR can only contribute credibly to a return below 1.5°C if peak warming remains well below 2°C and all residual emissions are reduced. Strong governance frameworks for CDR will be critical to allow responsible deployment and manage implications for environmental integrity, equity, scale.

Years of inaction mean that even if a return to below 1.5°C is secured, irreversible losses and permanently changed conditions are certain. Many communities may be forced to relocate or change livelihoods, while societies will face the challenge of re-adjustment. This raises issues of justice, power, and political legitimacy, which will require new, inclusive governance arrangements to resolve difficult issues.

This report is a reminder that an overshoot, peak and decline pathway is a next generation climate frontier, but one which cannot be left unattended to for the next generation to tackle. Immediate action is required for such a pathway to remain possible.
